name.text: NEETUG_PHYSICS_CLASS11_CH02_ST3_Q04 - Average velocity stopping distance and relative speed

questiontext.text:
Given below are three statements regarding kinematic relationships in straight-line motion:

Statement I: The relation for average velocity \(\bar{v} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}\) is universally valid for any straight-line motion, even when the acceleration varies with time.

Statement II: If a vehicle moving with initial speed \(v_0\) is brought to rest by applying a constant retarding force, the stopping distance is inversely proportional to the initial speed \(v_0\).

Statement III: When two objects \(A\) and \(B\) move along parallel straight paths in opposite directions with constant speeds \(v_A\) and \(v_B\) respectively, the magnitude of the relative velocity of \(A\) with respect to \(B\) is equal to \(v_A + v_B\).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

सरल रेखा में गति के शुद्धगतिक संबंधों के संदर्भ में नीचे तीन कथन दिए गए हैं:

कथन I: औसत वेग का संबंध \(\bar{v} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}\) किसी भी सरल रेखीय गति के लिए सार्वभौमिक रूप से मान्य है, भले ही त्वरण समय के साथ परिवर्तित हो रहा हो।

कथन II: यदि प्रारंभिक चाल \(v_0\) से गतिमान किसी वाहन को नियत मंदक बल लगाकर रोका जाता है, तो अवरोधन दूरी (रुकने की दूरी) प्रारंभिक चाल \(v_0\) के व्युत्क्रमानुपाती होती है।

कथन III: जब दो वस्तुएं \(A\) और \(B\) समांतर सीधी पटरियों पर विपरीत दिशाओं में क्रमशः नियत चालों \(v_A\) तथा \(v_B\) से गति करती हैं, तो \(B\) के सापेक्ष \(A\) के आपेक्षिक वेग का परिमाण \(v_A + v_B\) के बराबर होता है।

उपर्युक्त कथनों के आलोक में, नीचे दिए गए विकल्पों में से सही उत्तर चुनें:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Evaluation of the claim regarding the formula for average velocity
By definition, average velocity is total displacement divided by total time: \(\bar{v} = \frac{x - x_0}{t}\). For uniformly accelerated motion where velocity changes linearly (\(v = v_0 + at\)), integration gives \(x - x_0 = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = \left(\frac{v_0 + (v_0 + at)}{2}\right)t = \left(\frac{v_0 + v}{2}\right)t\), making \(\bar{v} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}\). However, when acceleration is non-uniform (time-dependent), velocity is not a linear function of time, and the arithmetic mean \(\frac{v_0 + v}{2}\) fails to equal the true average velocity \(\frac{1}{t}\int_0^t v(t)\, dt\). Thus, the relation is not universally valid. Hence, this claim is incorrect.

Step 2: Evaluation of the claim regarding the dependence of stopping distance on initial speed
Consider a vehicle with initial velocity \(v_0\) subjected to a constant retardation \(a\). When it comes to rest, final velocity is \(v = 0\). Applying the kinematic equation \(v^2 = v_0^2 - 2a d_s\) yields \(0 = v_0^2 - 2a d_s\), which gives the stopping distance \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\). This demonstrates that for a given constant braking retardation, stopping distance is directly proportional to the square of initial speed (\(d_s \propto v_0^2\)), rather than inversely proportional to \(v_0\). Thus, this claim is incorrect.

Step 3: Evaluation of the claim regarding relative velocity in opposite directions
Let the positive direction be along the velocity of object \(A\), so its velocity vector is \(\vec{v}_A = +v_A \hat{i}\). Since object \(B\) moves in the opposite direction, its velocity vector is \(\vec{v}_B = -v_B \hat{i}\). The relative velocity of \(A\) with respect to \(B\) is defined as \(\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B = v_A \hat{i} - (-v_B \hat{i}) = (v_A + v_B)\hat{i}\). Taking the magnitude yields \(|\vec{v}_{AB}| = v_A + v_B\). Hence, when moving in opposite directions, their relative speed is the sum of their individual speeds. Thus, this claim is physically sound.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The claims regarding the universal validity of the average velocity formula and the inverse dependence of stopping distance are both incorrect, while the claim regarding relative velocity for oppositely directed bodies is correct. Therefore, only the proposition regarding relative speed in opposite directions is correct.

चरण 1: औसत वेग के सूत्र की सार्वभौमिकता संबंधी दावे का मूल्यांकन
औसत वेग कुल विस्थापन और कुल समय का अनुपात होता है: \(\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\)। एकसमान त्वरित गति के लिए जहाँ वेग समय के साथ रैखिक रूप से बदलता है, \(\bar{v} = \frac{v_0 + v}{2}\) सत्य होता है। परंतु यदि त्वरण समय के साथ परिवर्ती हो, तो वेग समय का रैखिक फलन नहीं होता और समाकलन \(\frac{1}{t}\int_0^t v(t)\, dt\) का मान \(\frac{v_0 + v}{2}\) के बराबर नहीं आता। अतः यह संबंध केवल नियत त्वरण के लिए सत्य है, सार्वभौमिक नहीं। इसलिए यह दावा असत्य है।

चरण 2: अवरोधन दूरी की चाल पर निर्भरता संबंधी दावे का मूल्यांकन
नियत मंदन \(a\) के अधीन रुकने वाले वाहन के लिए अंतिम वेग \(v = 0\) होता है। गति के तृतीय समीकरण \(v^2 = v_0^2 - 2a d_s\) से \(0 = v_0^2 - 2a d_s\) प्राप्त होता है, जिससे अवरोधन दूरी \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\) मिलती है। यह दर्शाता है कि अवरोधन दूरी प्रारंभिक चाल के वर्ग के सीधे समानुपाती (\(d_s \propto v_0^2\)) होती है, न कि व्युत्क्रमानुपाती। इसलिए यह दावा असत्य है।

चरण 3: विपरीत दिशाओं में आपेक्षिक वेग संबंधी दावे का मूल्यांकन
यदि \(A\) की गति की दिशा को धनात्मक माना जाए, तो उसका वेग \(\vec{v}_A = +v_A \hat{i}\) तथा विपरीत दिशा में गतिमान \(B\) का वेग \(\vec{v}_B = -v_B \hat{i}\) होगा। \(B\) के सापेक्ष \(A\) का आपेक्षिक वेग \(\vec{v}_{AB} = \vec{v}_A - \vec{v}_B = v_A \hat{i} - (-v_B \hat{i}) = (v_A + v_B)\hat{i}\) होता है। इसका परिमाण \(|\vec{v}_{AB}| = v_A + v_B\) है। अतः विपरीत दिशाओं में चलने पर आपेक्षिक चाल दोनों चालों के योग के बराबर होती है। इसलिए यह दावा सत्य है।

चरण 4: जांच और अंतिम निष्कर्ष
मूल्यांकन से स्पष्ट है कि औसत वेग के सार्वभौमिक होने तथा अवरोधन दूरी के व्युत्क्रमानुपाती होने के दावे असत्य हैं, जबकि विपरीत दिशा में आपेक्षिक चाल के योग के बराबर होने का दावा सत्य है। अतः केवल विपरीत दिशा में आपेक्षिक चाल संबंधी दावा ही सत्य है।

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q01 - Definitions and mathematical forms of kinematic quantities

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Physical Quantity) with Column II (Mathematical Definition):

Column I (Physical Quantity) Column II (Mathematical Definition)
(A) Instantaneous velocity(I) \(\lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\)
(B) Average velocity(II) \(x(t_2) - x(t_1)\)
(C) Instantaneous acceleration(III) \(\lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\)
(D) Displacement(IV) \(\frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In kinematics along a straight coordinate axis, each physical quantity possesses a rigorous mathematical definition in terms of position coordinate \(x(t)\), velocity \(v(t)\), and time \(t\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Instantaneous Velocity
Instantaneous velocity is the time rate of change of position at a specific instant, defined as the differential limit \(v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\). This pairs instantaneous velocity with the differential limit of position.

Step 3: Evaluation of Average Velocity
Average velocity over a time interval from \(t_1\) to \(t_2\) is the net displacement divided by the elapsed time, \(\bar{v} = \frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}\). This pairs average velocity with the quotient of total position change over elapsed time.

Step 4: Evaluation of Instantaneous Acceleration
Instantaneous acceleration is the time rate of change of velocity at an instant, defined as \(a = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\). This pairs instantaneous acceleration with the differential limit of velocity.

Step 5: Evaluation of Displacement and Final Conclusion
Displacement is the change in the position coordinate of the particle between initial and final instants, \(\Delta x = x(t_2) - x(t_1)\). Combining all four pairings yields the complete set: instantaneous velocity pairs with the differential limit of position, average velocity pairs with the ratio of position difference to time difference, instantaneous acceleration pairs with the differential limit of velocity, and displacement pairs with the difference between final and initial coordinates. This corresponds to A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q02 - Interpretation of slopes and areas of graphs

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Graphical Feature) with Column II (Physical Meaning):

Column I (Graphical Feature) Column II (Physical Meaning)
(A) Slope of the tangent to position–time curve(I) Motion with positive acceleration
(B) Area bounded under velocity–time curve and time axis(II) Instantaneous acceleration
(C) Slope of the tangent to velocity–time curve(III) Displacement over the time interval
(D) Upward-bending curvature on position–time curve(IV) Instantaneous velocity

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kinematic graphs visually encapsulate the calculus relationships between position \(x\), velocity \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\), and acceleration \(a = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\). Derivatives correspond to slopes of tangents, definite integrals correspond to enclosed areas, and second derivatives determine concavity.

Step 2: Evaluation of Position–Time Slope
The derivative \(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\) is geometrically represented by the slope of the tangent to the position–time curve, giving the instantaneous velocity. Thus, the slope of the position–time curve pairs with instantaneous velocity.

Step 3: Evaluation of Velocity–Time Area
The definite integral \(\int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\) geometrically corresponds to the area enclosed between the velocity–time curve and the time axis, representing the net displacement. Thus, the area under the velocity–time curve pairs with displacement over the time interval.

Step 4: Evaluation of Velocity–Time Slope
The derivative \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\) is geometrically represented by the slope of the tangent to the velocity–time curve, giving the instantaneous acceleration. Thus, the slope of the velocity–time curve pairs with instantaneous acceleration.

Step 5: Evaluation of Curvature and Final Conclusion
The second derivative \(\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\) determines the concavity of the position–time curve: a curve that is concave upward (curves upward) signifies \(\frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2} > 0\), which corresponds to positive acceleration. Combining all four pairs yields: position–time slope matches instantaneous velocity, velocity–time area matches displacement, velocity–time slope matches instantaneous acceleration, and upward curvature matches positive acceleration. This corresponds to A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q03 - Kinematic parameters and analytical mathematical formulas

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Kinematic Parameter) with Column II (Analytical Expression):

Column I (Kinematic Parameter) Column II (Analytical Expression)
(A) Stopping distance under uniform braking retardation \(a\)(I) \(\sqrt{2gh}\)
(B) Distance traversed in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) second under uniform gravity from rest(II) \(\frac{v_0^2}{2a}\)
(C) Speed acquired falling freely through height \(h\) from rest(III) \(v_0 t_r\)
(D) Distance traversed during reaction time \(t_r\) at constant speed \(v_0\)(IV) \(\frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Uniformly accelerated motion is governed by the kinematic equations \(v = v_0 + at\), \(x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}at^2\), and \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax\). Specific physical boundary conditions yield characteristic expressions for stopping distance, nth-second displacement, free fall velocity, and reaction travel.

Step 2: Evaluation of Stopping Distance
For a vehicle brought to rest from initial speed \(v_0\) under constant deceleration \(a\), setting final speed \(v = 0\) in \(v^2 = v_0^2 - 2a d_s\) gives stopping distance \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\). Thus, stopping distance pairs with \(\frac{v_0^2}{2a}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Distance in the nth Second
For an object released from rest (\(u = 0\)) under uniform gravitational acceleration \(g\), the distance covered in the \(n^{\text{th}}\) second is \(s_n = u + \frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1) = \frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\). Thus, distance in the nth second pairs with \(\frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\).

Step 4: Evaluation of Speed after Free Fall
For free fall from rest over height \(h\) under acceleration \(g\), using \(v^2 = 0 + 2gh\) yields final speed \(v = \sqrt{2gh}\). Thus, speed acquired falling through height \(h\) pairs with \(\sqrt{2gh}\).

Step 5: Evaluation of Reaction Distance and Final Conclusion
During the driver's reaction time \(t_r\), the brakes have not yet taken effect, so the car moves at constant initial speed \(v_0\). The distance traveled is \(d = v_0 t_r\). Thus, reaction distance pairs with \(v_0 t_r\). Combining all four pairs yields: stopping distance pairs with \(\frac{v_0^2}{2a}\), distance in the nth second pairs with \(\frac{1}{2}g(2n - 1)\), speed acquired in free fall pairs with \(\sqrt{2gh}\), and reaction distance pairs with \(v_0 t_r\). This corresponds to A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_CLASS_11_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MATCH_Q04 - Motion characteristics matched to velocity time profiles

questiontext.text:
Match Column I (Physical Motion Description) with Column II (Velocity–Time Graph Characteristics):

Column I (Physical Motion Description) Column II (Velocity–Time Graph Characteristics)
(A) Motion in positive direction with uniform positive acceleration(I) Straight line with negative slope intersecting the time axis to enter the negative velocity region
(B) Motion in positive direction with uniform negative acceleration reversing direction(II) Straight line parallel to the time axis with zero slope
(C) Free fall from rest in negative direction under constant downward gravity(III) Straight line starting at positive initial velocity with positive slope rising upward
(D) Rectilinear motion with uniform velocity and zero acceleration(IV) Straight line starting from the origin with constant negative slope descending into negative velocities

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Consider rectilinear motion described by velocity \(v(t) = v_0 + at\). On a \(v\)–\(t\) Cartesian plot, the initial velocity \(v_0\) represents the vertical intercept at \(t = 0\), and the acceleration \(a\) represents the constant slope \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 2: Evaluation of Positive Direction with Positive Acceleration
Here, initial velocity is positive (\(v_0 > 0\)) and acceleration is positive (\(a > 0\)). The \(v\)–\(t\) curve begins on the positive vertical axis and slopes upward with positive slope, representing a straight line starting at positive velocity and rising upward. Thus, this motion pairs with the rising straight line with positive slope.

Step 3: Evaluation of Positive Motion Reversing under Negative Acceleration
Here, the initial velocity is positive (\(v_0 > 0\)) but acceleration is negative (\(a < 0\)). The velocity decreases linearly, passes through zero when the particle momentarily turns back at the time axis, and continues downward into negative velocity values. Thus, this motion pairs with the straight line with negative slope that intersects the time axis to enter negative velocities.

Step 4: Evaluation of Free Fall from Rest in Negative Direction
Choosing the upward direction as positive, a body dropped from rest has \(v_0 = 0\) and constant downward acceleration \(a = -g\). The velocity is given by \(v(t) = -gt\), which starts at the origin and slopes downward linearly into the negative velocity region. Thus, this motion pairs with the straight line starting from the origin with constant negative slope.

Step 5: Evaluation of Zero Acceleration and Final Conclusion
When acceleration is zero (\(a = 0\)), the velocity is constant: \(v(t) = u\). The rate of change \(\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0\), producing a horizontal straight line parallel to the time axis. Thus, zero acceleration pairs with the line parallel to the time axis. Combining all four pairs yields: positive motion with positive acceleration pairs with the rising positive-slope line, reversal under negative acceleration pairs with the line crossing the time axis, free fall from rest pairs with the line descending from the origin into negative values, and uniform velocity pairs with the line parallel to the time axis. This corresponds to A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q01 - Initial velocity from quadratic position relation

questiontext.text: The position of a particle moving along the \(x\)-axis is given by \(x = a + bt^2\), where \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), and \(t\) is in seconds. What is the velocity of the particle at \(t = 0\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position function: \(x(t) = a + bt^2\) with \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\) and \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Evaluation instant: \(t = 0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position: \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiating the position equation with respect to time:
\[v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(a + bt^2) = 2bt\]
Substituting \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(t = 0\text{ s}\):
\[v(0) = 2 \times 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \times 0\text{ s} = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The initial velocity at \(t = 0\text{ s}\) is \(0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
0 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q02 - Instantaneous velocity at two seconds

questiontext.text: The position of an object moving along the \(x\)-axis is described by \(x = a + bt^2\), where \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), and \(t\) is in seconds. What is the instantaneous velocity of the object at \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position function: \(x(t) = a + bt^2\) with \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Instant: \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Instantaneous velocity is given by \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiating position with respect to time:
\[v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(a + bt^2) = 2bt\]
Evaluating at \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\):
\[v(2.0) = 2 \times 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \times 2.0\text{ s} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The instantaneous velocity at \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\) is \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
10 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q03 - Average velocity across time interval

questiontext.text: The position of an object moving along the \(x\)-axis is given by \(x = a + bt^2\), where \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), and \(t\) is in seconds. What is the average velocity of the object between \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\) and \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position relation: \(x(t) = a + bt^2\) with \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Time interval: from \(t_1 = 2.0\text{ s}\) to \(t_2 = 4.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average velocity is given by the net displacement divided by the elapsed time:
\[\bar{v} = \frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Evaluate positions:
\[x(2.0) = a + b(2.0)^2 = a + 4b\]
\[x(4.0) = a + b(4.0)^2 = a + 16b\]
Calculate displacement:
\[\Delta x = x(4.0) - x(2.0) = (a + 16b) - (a + 4b) = 12b\]
The elapsed time is \(\Delta t = 4.0\text{ s} - 2.0\text{ s} = 2.0\text{ s}\).
Evaluate average velocity:
\[\bar{v} = \frac{12b}{2.0} = 6.0b = 6.0 \times 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2} = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The average velocity over the given interval is \(15\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
15 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q04 - Instantaneous velocity from cubic position function

questiontext.text: A car moves along a straight line such that its position is given by \(x = 0.08 t^3\), where \(x\) is in meters and \(t\) is in seconds. What is the instantaneous velocity of the car at \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position function: \(x(t) = 0.08 t^3\). Time instant: \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Instantaneous velocity is the time derivative of position: \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiating position with respect to time:
\[v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(0.08 t^3) = 3 \times 0.08 t^2 = 0.24 t^2\]
Evaluating at \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\):
\[v(4.0) = 0.24 \times (4.0)^2 = 0.24 \times 16 = 3.84\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The instantaneous velocity at \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\) is \(3.84\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
3.84 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q05 - Average velocity over two second interval

questiontext.text: For the motion of a car where position varies as \(x = 0.08 t^3\) (with \(x\) in meters and \(t\) in seconds), what is the average velocity over the time interval from \(t = 3.0\text{ s}\) to \(t = 5.0\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position relation: \(x(t) = 0.08 t^3\). Time limits: \(t_1 = 3.0\text{ s}\), \(t_2 = 5.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average velocity is defined as \(\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate position at \(t_1 = 3.0\text{ s}\):
\[x(3.0) = 0.08 \times (3.0)^3 = 0.08 \times 27 = 2.16\text{ m}\]
Calculate position at \(t_2 = 5.0\text{ s}\):
\[x(5.0) = 0.08 \times (5.0)^3 = 0.08 \times 125 = 10.0\text{ m}\]
Calculate net displacement:
\[\Delta x = 10.0\text{ m} - 2.16\text{ m} = 7.84\text{ m}\]
Calculate elapsed time:
\[\Delta t = 5.0\text{ s} - 3.0\text{ s} = 2.0\text{ s}\]
Evaluate average velocity:
\[\bar{v} = \frac{7.84\text{ m}}{2.0\text{ s}} = 3.92\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The average velocity over this interval is \(3.92\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
3.92 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q06 - Acceleration at momentary rest instant

questiontext.text: A particle moves along a straight line such that its displacement varies with time as \(x(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t\), where \(x\) is in meters and \(t\) is in seconds. What is the magnitude of the acceleration of the particle at the instant when it comes to rest for the first time after \(t = 0\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position function: \(x(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t\). Condition: first instant of momentary rest (\(v = 0\)) for \(t > 0\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Velocity is \(v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\). Acceleration is \(a(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 x}{\mathrm{d}t^2}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Find velocity by differentiating position:
\[v(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t) = 6t^2 - 18t + 12\]
Set \(v(t) = 0\) to find the instants of rest:
\[6(t^2 - 3t + 2) = 0 \implies (t - 1)(t - 2) = 0\]
The particle comes to rest at \(t = 1\text{ s}\) and \(t = 2\text{ s}\). The first instant after \(t = 0\) is \(t = 1\text{ s}\).
Differentiate velocity to find acceleration:
\[a(t) = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(6t^2 - 18t + 12) = 12t - 18\]
Evaluating at \(t = 1\text{ s}\):
\[a(1) = 12(1) - 18 = -6\text{ m s}^{-2}\]
The magnitude of the acceleration is \(6\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The magnitude of the acceleration at the first instant of rest is \(6\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Answer:
6 m s^{-2}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q07 - Average velocity on closed market path

questiontext.text: A man walks along a straight road from his home to a market \(2.5\text{ km}\) away with a speed of \(5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Finding the market closed, he instantly turns around and walks back home with a speed of \(7.5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). What is the magnitude of his average velocity over the time interval from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 50\text{ min}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Outward distance: \(2.5\text{ km}\) at \(5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Return distance: \(2.5\text{ km}\) at \(7.5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Time interval: \(50\text{ min}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average velocity is net displacement divided by total time: \(\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Outward time: \(t_1 = \frac{2.5\text{ km}}{5\text{ km h}^{-1}} = 0.5\text{ h} = 30\text{ min}\).
Return time: \(t_2 = \frac{2.5\text{ km}}{7.5\text{ km h}^{-1}} = \frac{1}{3}\text{ h} = 20\text{ min}\).
Total time for the round trip is \(30\text{ min} + 20\text{ min} = 50\text{ min}\).
At \(t = 50\text{ min}\), the man is back at his initial position (home).
The net displacement is \(\Delta x = 0\text{ km}\).
Thus, \(\bar{v} = \frac{0}{50\text{ min}} = 0\text{ km h}^{-1}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Since the net displacement is zero, the average velocity is \(0\text{ km h}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
0 km h^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q08 - Average speed on full market journey

questiontext.text: A man walks along a straight road from his home to a market \(2.5\text{ km}\) away with a speed of \(5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Finding the market closed, he instantly turns around and walks back home with a speed of \(7.5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). What is his average speed over the total duration of \(50\text{ min}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Outward distance: \(2.5\text{ km}\) at \(5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Return distance: \(2.5\text{ km}\) at \(7.5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Total elapsed time: \(50\text{ min} = \frac{5}{6}\text{ h}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average speed is total path length divided by total elapsed time: \(\bar{v}_{\text{speed}} = \frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Total distance covered is \(2.5\text{ km} + 2.5\text{ km} = 5.0\text{ km}\).
Total elapsed time is \(50\text{ min} = \frac{50}{60}\text{ h} = \frac{5}{6}\text{ h}\).
Evaluating average speed:
\[\bar{v}_{\text{speed}} = \frac{5.0\text{ km}}{\frac{5}{6}\text{ h}} = 5.0 \times \frac{6}{5} = 6.0\text{ km h}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The average speed over the \(50\text{ min}\) interval is \(6.0\text{ km h}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
6.0 km h^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q09 - Average speed across forty minute span

questiontext.text: A man walks on a straight road from home to a market \(2.5\text{ km}\) away with a speed of \(5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Finding the market closed, he instantly turns around and walks back home with a speed of \(7.5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). What is his average speed over the time interval from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 40\text{ min}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Outward journey: \(2.5\text{ km}\) at \(5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Return speed: \(7.5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Target time interval: \(40\text{ min} = \frac{2}{3}\text{ h}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average speed is \(\bar{v}_{\text{speed}} = \frac{\text{Total Path Length}}{\text{Total Time}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Time taken to reach the market: \(t_1 = \frac{2.5\text{ km}}{5\text{ km h}^{-1}} = 0.5\text{ h} = 30\text{ min}\).
Remaining time in the interval: \(\Delta t = 40\text{ min} - 30\text{ min} = 10\text{ min} = \frac{1}{6}\text{ h}\).
Distance covered during return in \(10\text{ min}\):
\[d_2 = 7.5\text{ km h}^{-1} \times \frac{1}{6}\text{ h} = 1.25\text{ km}\]
Total distance covered in \(40\text{ min}\):
\[d_{\text{total}} = 2.5\text{ km} + 1.25\text{ km} = 3.75\text{ km}\]
Evaluating average speed:
\[\bar{v}_{\text{speed}} = \frac{3.75\text{ km}}{\frac{2}{3}\text{ h}} = 3.75 \times 1.5 = 5.625\text{ km h}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The average speed over the \(40\text{ min}\) interval is \(5.625\text{ km h}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
5.625 km h^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q10 - Total travel time of walking and auto journey

questiontext.text: A woman walks on a straight road from her home to her office \(2.5\text{ km}\) away with a speed of \(5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). After staying at the office, she returns home by an auto with a speed of \(25\text{ km h}^{-1}\). What is the total travel time spent by the woman on the road for the round trip?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
One-way distance: \(d = 2.5\text{ km}\). Walking speed: \(v_1 = 5\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Auto speed: \(v_2 = 25\text{ km h}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Time taken is distance divided by speed: \(t = \frac{d}{v}\). Total travel time is \(T = t_1 + t_2\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Time taken walking to office:
\[t_1 = \frac{2.5\text{ km}}{5\text{ km h}^{-1}} = 0.5\text{ h} = 30\text{ min}\]
Time taken returning by auto:
\[t_2 = \frac{2.5\text{ km}}{25\text{ km h}^{-1}} = 0.1\text{ h} = 6\text{ min}\]
Total travel time:
\[T = 30\text{ min} + 6\text{ min} = 36\text{ min} = 0.6\text{ h}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The total transit time is \(36\text{ min}\) (or \(0.6\text{ h}\)).

Final Answer:
36 min

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q11 - Magnitude of uniform vehicle retardation

questiontext.text: A car moving along a straight highway with a speed of \(126\text{ km h}^{-1}\) is brought to a stop within a distance of \(200\text{ m}\) under uniform braking. What is the magnitude of the retardation of the car?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed: \(v_0 = 126\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Final speed: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Stopping distance: \(x = 200\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Convert initial speed to SI units: \(v_0 = 126 \\times \frac{5}{18}\text{ m s}^{-1} = 35\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Using kinematic equation: \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2ax\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the parameters:
\[0 = (35)^2 + 2a(200)\]
\[0 = 1225 + 400a\]
\[400a = -1225 \implies a = -3.0625\text{ m s}^{-2}\]
The magnitude of retardation is \(3.06\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The retardation of the car is \(3.06\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Final Answer:
3.06 m s^{-2}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q12 - Stopping time under constant retardation

questiontext.text: A car traveling at \(126\text{ km h}^{-1}\) on a straight road is brought to a complete stop within \(200\text{ m}\) under uniform deceleration. How long does it take for the car to stop?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed: \(v_0 = 126\text{ km h}^{-1} = 35\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Final speed: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Distance: \(x = 200\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Displacement under constant acceleration is \(x = \left(\frac{v_0 + v}{2}\right)t\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[200 = \left(\frac{35 + 0}{2}\right)t\]
\[200 = 17.5\,t \implies t = \frac{200}{17.5} = \frac{80}{7} \approx 11.43\text{ s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The car takes approximately \(11.4\text{ s}\) to stop.

Final Answer:
11.4 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q13 - Ratio of stopping distances on doubling speed

questiontext.text: A vehicle moving with an initial speed of \(11\text{ m s}^{-1}\) comes to rest in a distance \(d_1\) under constant braking deceleration. If the same vehicle moves with an initial speed of \(22\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and undergoes the same deceleration, it comes to rest in distance \(d_2\). What is the ratio \(\frac{d_2}{d_1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speeds: \(v_1 = 11\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and \(v_2 = 22\text{ m s}^{-1} = 2v_1\). Deceleration \(a\) is constant.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Stopping distance is given by \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Since stopping distance is proportional to the square of initial speed:
\[d_s \propto v_0^2\]
Forming the ratio:
\[\frac{d_2}{d_1} = \left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{22}{11}\right)^2 = (2)^2 = 4\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ratio of the stopping distances is \(4 : 1\).

Final Answer:
4 : 1

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q14 - Stopping distance extrapolation from empirical braking

questiontext.text: For a particular automobile, the braking distance is measured to be \(34.0\text{ m}\) when traveling at an initial speed of \(20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Assuming the same constant braking deceleration, what is the stopping distance when the vehicle travels at \(25.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed \(v_1 = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\), stopping distance \(d_1 = 34.0\text{ m}\). New initial speed \(v_2 = 25.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Braking deceleration is constant.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Stopping distance is proportional to the square of initial speed: \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Using the ratio relation:
\[\frac{d_2}{d_1} = \left(\frac{v_2}{v_1}\right)^2\]
Substitute the numerical values:
\[d_2 = 34.0 \times \left(\frac{25.0}{20.0}\right)^2 = 34.0 \times (1.25)^2 = 34.0 \times 1.5625 = 53.125\text{ m} \approx 53.1\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The new stopping distance is approximately \(53.1\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
53.1 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q15 - Distance covered in sixth second with reversal

questiontext.text: A particle moves along a straight line with an initial velocity of \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and a constant retardation of \(2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). What is the total distance covered by the particle during the 6th second of its motion (from \(t = 5.0\text{ s}\) to \(t = 6.0\text{ s}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Retardation: \(a = -2.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Time interval of interest: \(t = 5.0\text{ s}\) to \(t = 6.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Velocity at any instant is \(v(t) = v_0 + at\). The particle reverses direction when \(v = 0\). Distance is the absolute path length.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Find when the particle comes momentarily to rest:
\[0 = 10 - 2.0\,t \implies t = 5.0\text{ s}\]
At \(t = 5.0\text{ s}\), the particle reaches its farthest point and starts moving in the opposite direction.
Between \(t = 5.0\text{ s}\) and \(t = 6.0\text{ s}\), the particle accelerates from rest (at \(t = 5.0\text{ s}\)) in the negative direction.
The distance covered in this \(1.0\text{ s}\) interval is:
\[d = \frac{1}{2}|a|(\Delta t)^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2.0\text{ m s}^{-2})(1.0\text{ s})^2 = 1.0\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The total distance covered during the 6th second is \(1.0\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
1.0 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q16 - Distance in fifth second from third second data

questiontext.text: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration along a straight line. If the distance covered by the body in the 3rd second of its motion is \(15.0\text{ m}\), what distance will it cover in the 5th second?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 0\). Distance in 3rd second: \(s_3 = 15.0\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Distance covered in the \(n\)-th second from rest is \(s_n = \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
For \(n = 3\):
\[s_3 = \frac{a}{2}(2 \times 3 - 1) = \frac{5a}{2} = 15.0\text{ m}\]
Solving for acceleration:
\[5a = 30.0 \implies a = 6.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\]
Now find the distance covered in the 5th second (\(n = 5\)):
\[s_5 = \frac{a}{2}(2 \times 5 - 1) = \frac{6.0}{2}(9) = 3.0 \times 9 = 27.0\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The distance covered in the 5th second is \(27.0\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
27.0 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q17 - Total displacement in three phase motion

questiontext.text: A vehicle accelerates uniformly from rest to a speed of \(72.0\text{ km h}^{-1}\) in \(10.0\text{ s}\), then moves with this constant speed for \(20.0\text{ s}\), and finally comes to rest under uniform retardation in \(5.0\text{ s}\). What is the total distance traversed by the vehicle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Phase 1: from rest to \(72.0\text{ km h}^{-1}\) in \(t_1 = 10.0\text{ s}\). Phase 2: constant speed for \(t_2 = 20.0\text{ s}\). Phase 3: to rest in \(t_3 = 5.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Convert speed: \(v = 72.0 \times \frac{5}{18}\text{ m s}^{-1} = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph (a trapezoid):
\[x_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}(t_{\text{top}} + t_{\text{base}})v_{\text{max}}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Base of trapezoid: \(T = 10.0 + 20.0 + 5.0 = 35.0\text{ s}\).
Top of trapezoid (constant speed phase): \(t_2 = 20.0\text{ s}\).
Maximum speed: \(v_{\text{max}} = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Evaluating the total distance:
\[x_{\text{total}} = \frac{1}{2}(20.0\text{ s} + 35.0\text{ s}) \times 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}(55.0) \times 20.0 = 550.0\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The total distance traversed during the entire journey is \(550.0\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
550.0 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q18 - Displacement calculated from vt graph geometry

questiontext.text: A particle starts with an initial velocity \(v_0 = 12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) and accelerates uniformly to \(v = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) in a time duration of \(4.0\text{ s}\). Using the area under the velocity-time graph, what is the displacement of the particle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Final velocity: \(v = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Time duration: \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Area under \(v\)-\(t\) graph is the area of a rectangle plus a triangle:
\[x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2}(v - v_0)t\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate the rectangular area:
\[A_{\text{rect}} = v_0 t = 12.0\text{ m s}^{-1} \times 4.0\text{ s} = 48.0\text{ m}\]
Calculate the triangular area:
\[A_{\text{tri}} = \frac{1}{2}(20.0 - 12.0)\text{ m s}^{-1} \times 4.0\text{ s} = \frac{1}{2}(8.0) \times 4.0 = 16.0\text{ m}\]
Total displacement:
\[x = 48.0\text{ m} + 16.0\text{ m} = 64.0\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The displacement is \(64.0\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
64.0 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q19 - Rise height above launch point

questiontext.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with an initial velocity of \(20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) from the roof of a building \(25.0\text{ m}\) high. Taking \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\), how high above the launch point does the ball rise?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Velocity at highest point: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Acceleration: \(a = -g = -10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Using the third kinematic equation: \(v^2 = v_0^2 - 2g(y - y_0)\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[0 = (20.0)^2 - 2(10.0)(y - y_0)\]
\[20.0(y - y_0) = 400.0 \implies y - y_0 = 20.0\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ball rises \(20.0\text{ m}\) above its point of launch.

Final Answer:
20.0 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q20 - Maximum height of ball above ground level

questiontext.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with an initial velocity of \(20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) from the top of a building \(25.0\text{ m}\) high. Taking \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the maximum height attained by the ball above the ground?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Launch height above ground: \(y_0 = 25.0\text{ m}\). Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Maximum height above ground is the launch height plus rise height: \(y_{\text{max}} = y_0 + \frac{v_0^2}{2g}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate rise height:
\[h_{\text{rise}} = \frac{(20.0)^2}{2(10.0)} = \frac{400.0}{20.0} = 20.0\text{ m}\]
Total height above ground:
\[y_{\text{max}} = 25.0\text{ m} + 20.0\text{ m} = 45.0\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The maximum height above the ground is \(45.0\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
45.0 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q21 - Time to apex of vertical throw from roof

questiontext.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with a velocity of \(20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) from the roof of a building \(25.0\text{ m}\) high. Taking \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\), how much time elapses before the ball reaches its highest point?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Apex velocity: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Acceleration: \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Using \(v = v_0 - gt\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Setting velocity to zero:
\[0 = 20.0 - 10.0\,t_1 \implies 10.0\,t_1 = 20.0 \implies t_1 = 2.0\text{ s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The time taken to reach the apex is \(2.0\text{ s}\).

Final Answer:
2.0 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q22 - Descent time from apex to ground

questiontext.text: A ball reaches a maximum height of \(45.0\text{ m}\) above the ground after being thrown upward from a building. Taking \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\), how long does it take for the ball to fall freely from this highest point to the ground?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed at apex: \(v_0 = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Height fallen: \(H = 45.0\text{ m}\). Acceleration: \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For free fall from rest: \(H = \frac{1}{2}gt_2^2 \implies t_2 = \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the parameters:
\[t_2 = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 45.0\text{ m}}{10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{90.0}{10.0}} = \sqrt{9.0} = 3.0\text{ s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The descent time from the apex to the ground is \(3.0\text{ s}\).

Final Answer:
3.0 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q23 - Total flight duration of projectile from building

questiontext.text: A ball is launched vertically upwards at \(20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) from the roof of a \(25.0\text{ m}\) tall building. Taking \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the total time elapsed before the ball hits the ground?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Launch position: \(y_0 = 25.0\text{ m}\). Final ground position: \(y = 0\text{ m}\). Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Acceleration: \(a = -10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Total flight time is the sum of upward time and downward time: \(T = t_1 + t_2\). Alternatively, solve \(y = y_0 + v_0 t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Using the quadratic equation for displacement:
\[0 = 25.0 + 20.0t - 5.0t^2\]
\[5t^2 - 20t - 25 = 0 \implies t^2 - 4t - 5 = 0\]
\[(t - 5)(t + 1) = 0\]
Since time must be positive, \(t = 5.0\text{ s}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The total flight time is \(5.0\text{ s}\).

Final Answer:
5.0 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q24 - Impact speed of ball on ground surface

questiontext.text: A ball is thrown vertically upwards with an initial speed of \(20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) from the top of a building \(25.0\text{ m}\) high. Taking \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\), with what speed does the ball strike the ground?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 20.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Launch height: \(h = 25.0\text{ m}\). Acceleration: \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Using energy conservation or third kinematic equation: \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2gh\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values:
\[v^2 = (20.0)^2 + 2(10.0)(25.0) = 400.0 + 500.0 = 900.0\text{ m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}\]
Taking the square root:
\[v = \sqrt{900.0} = 30.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The striking speed of the ball is \(30.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
30.0 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q25 - Time to peak for vertical toss

questiontext.text: A player throws a ball vertically upwards with an initial speed of \(29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Neglecting air resistance and taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the time taken by the ball to reach its highest point?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed: \(v_0 = 29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Final speed at peak: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Using \(v = v_0 - gt\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the parameters:
\[0 = 29.4 - 9.8\,t \implies t = \frac{29.4}{9.8} = 3.0\text{ s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The time taken to reach the apex is \(3.0\text{ s}\).

Final Answer:
3.0 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q26 - Total round trip time of thrown ball

questiontext.text: A player throws a ball vertically upwards with an initial speed of \(29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Neglecting air resistance and taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), after what total time does the ball return to the player's hands?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed: \(v_0 = 29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Net displacement on return: \(y = 0\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Time of ascent equals time of descent: \(T = 2 \times \frac{v_0}{g}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Time of ascent is \(t_{\text{up}} = \frac{29.4}{9.8} = 3.0\text{ s}\).
Total flight time:
\[T = 2 \times 3.0\text{ s} = 6.0\text{ s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ball returns to the player's hands after \(6.0\text{ s}\).

Final Answer:
6.0 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q27 - Maximum height achieved by vertical toss

questiontext.text: A player throws a ball vertically upwards with an initial speed of \(29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Neglecting air resistance and taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), to what maximum height does the ball rise?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 29.4\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Velocity at apex: \(v = 0\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Acceleration: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Maximum height is \(H = \frac{v_0^2}{2g}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values:
\[H = \frac{(29.4)^2}{2 \times 9.8} = \frac{(3 \\times 9.8)^2}{2 \times 9.8} = \frac{9 \times 9.8}{2} = 9 \times 4.9 = 44.1\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The maximum height attained is \(44.1\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
44.1 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q28 - Ratio of distances in successive equal intervals

questiontext.text: A stone falls freely from rest under gravity. What is the ratio of the distances traversed by the stone during the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd second of its fall?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 0\). Free fall under gravity with equal intervals \(\tau = 1.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
According to Galileo's law of odd numbers, the distance covered in the \(n\)-th second is proportional to \(2n - 1\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
For \(n = 1\): \(s_1 \propto 2(1) - 1 = 1\).
For \(n = 2\): \(s_2 \propto 2(2) - 1 = 3\).
For \(n = 3\): \(s_3 \propto 2(3) - 1 = 5\).
The ratio is \(s_1 : s_2 : s_3 = 1 : 3 : 5\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ratio of the distances covered in the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd second is \(1 : 3 : 5\).

Final Answer:
1 : 3 : 5

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q29 - Ratio of fifth second to second second distance

questiontext.text: A body falls freely from rest under gravity. What is the ratio of the distance traversed during the 5th second of its fall to the distance traversed during the 2nd second?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial speed: \(v_0 = 0\). Evaluation seconds: \(n_1 = 5\) and \(n_2 = 2\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The distance covered in the \(n\)-th second is \(s_n = \frac{g}{2}(2n - 1)\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Distance in 5th second:
\[s_5 = \frac{g}{2}(2 \times 5 - 1) = 9 \left(\frac{g}{2}\right)\]
Distance in 2nd second:
\[s_2 = \frac{g}{2}(2 \times 2 - 1) = 3 \left(\frac{g}{2}\right)\]
Forming the ratio:
\[\frac{s_5}{s_2} = \frac{9}{3} = 3 : 1\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ratio of distance fallen in the 5th second to that in the 2nd second is \(3 : 1\).

Final Answer:
3 : 1

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q30 - Reaction time from measured ruler displacement

questiontext.text: In a ruler-drop test to measure human reaction time, a student catches a vertically falling ruler after it has dropped through a distance of \(21.0\text{ cm}\) from rest. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the estimated reaction time?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Drop distance: \(d = 21.0\text{ cm} = 0.21\text{ m}\). Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 0\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
The reaction time is related to the drop distance by \(d = \frac{1}{2}gt_r^2 \implies t_r = \sqrt{\frac{2d}{g}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the values:
\[t_r = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 0.21\text{ m}}{9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.42}{9.8}} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{70}} \approx \sqrt{0.042857} \approx 0.207\text{ s} \approx 0.21\text{ s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The reaction time is approximately \(0.21\text{ s}\) (or \(\approx 0.2\text{ s}\)).

Final Answer:
0.21 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q31 - Drop distance corresponding to quarter second reaction

questiontext.text: If a person has a measured reaction time of \(0.25\text{ s}\), how far does a vertically falling ruler drop from rest before being caught? (Take \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\)).

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Reaction time: \(t_r = 0.25\text{ s}\). Gravitational acceleration: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Distance fallen from rest: \(d = \frac{1}{2}gt_r^2\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the parameters:
\[d = \frac{1}{2} \times 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \times (0.25\text{ s})^2 = 4.9 \times 0.0625 = 0.30625\text{ m} = 30.6\text{ cm}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ruler slips through a distance of \(30.6\text{ cm}\).

Final Answer:
30.6 cm

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q32 - Impact speed of ninety meter dropped ball

questiontext.text: A ball is released from rest from a height of \(90.0\text{ m}\) above a rigid floor. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the speed of the ball immediately before it collides with the floor?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Drop height: \(h = 90.0\text{ m}\). Initial velocity: \(v_0 = 0\). Acceleration: \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Using the kinematic formula: \(v_1 = \sqrt{2gh}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the numerical values:
\[v_1 = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2} \times 90.0\text{ m}} = \sqrt{19.6 \times 90.0} = \sqrt{1764} = 42.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The speed of the ball just prior to striking the floor is \(42.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
42.0 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q33 - Rebound height following ten percent speed reduction

questiontext.text: A ball is dropped from rest from a height of \(90.0\text{ m}\) onto a rigid floor. Upon bouncing, the ball loses one-tenth (\(10\%\)) of its speed. Taking \(g = 9.8\text{ m s}^{-2}\), to what height does the ball rise after the bounce?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial height: \(h_1 = 90.0\text{ m}\). Fraction of speed lost: \(10\%\), meaning rebound speed is \(v_2 = 0.9 v_1\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Rebound height is \(h_2 = \frac{v_2^2}{2g} = \frac{(0.9 v_1)^2}{2g} = (0.9)^2 h_1 = 0.81 h_1\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the initial height:
\[h_2 = 0.81 \times 90.0\text{ m} = 72.9\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The ball rebounds to a height of \(72.9\text{ m}\).

Final Answer:
72.9 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q34 - Position of intermediate falling drop

questiontext.text: Water drops fall at regular equal intervals of time from a tap located \(16.0\text{ m}\) above the ground. At the exact instant when the 5th drop is released, the 1st drop strikes the ground. Taking \(g = 10.0\text{ m s}^{-2}\), what is the height of the 2nd drop above the ground at that instant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Total height: \(H = 16.0\text{ m}\). The 1st drop strikes ground as 5th drop leaves, corresponding to \(5 - 1 = 4\) equal intervals \(\tau\). Target: height of 2nd drop above ground.

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Distance fallen from rest in \(k\) intervals is \(d_k = \frac{1}{2}g(k\tau)^2\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Total height fallen by 1st drop in \(4\tau\):
\[H = \frac{1}{2}g(4\tau)^2 = 16 \left(\frac{1}{2}g\tau^2\right) = 16.0\text{ m} \implies \frac{1}{2}g\tau^2 = 1.0\text{ m}\]
The 2nd drop was released at time \(t = \tau\) after the 1st drop, so at the moment the 5th drop is released (total time \(4\tau\)), the 2nd drop has been falling for \(3\tau\).
Distance fallen by 2nd drop:
\[d_2 = \frac{1}{2}g(3\tau)^2 = 9 \left(\frac{1}{2}g\tau^2\right) = 9 \times 1.0\text{ m} = 9.0\text{ m}\]
Height of the 2nd drop above the ground:
\[h_2 = 16.0\text{ m} - 9.0\text{ m} = 7.0\text{ m}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The 2nd drop is at a height of \(7.0\text{ m}\) above the ground.

Final Answer:
7.0 m

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q35 - Time to fall in pit during cyclic motion

questiontext.text: A drunkard walking in a narrow lane takes 5 steps forward followed by 3 steps backward, then 5 steps forward and 3 steps backward, and so on. Each step is \(1\text{ m}\) long and takes \(1\text{ s}\). How long does he take to fall into a pit located \(13\text{ m}\) ahead of his initial position?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Step length: \(1\text{ m}\). Step time: \(1\text{ s}\). Cycle: 5 forward, 3 backward. Pit distance: \(13\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Each full cycle of 8 steps takes \(8\text{ s}\) and produces a net displacement of \(5\text{ m} - 3\text{ m} = 2\text{ m}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
After 4 complete cycles (\(4 \times 8\text{ s} = 32\text{ s}\)), his net position is:
\[x_4 = 4 \times 2\text{ m} = 8\text{ m}\]
From \(x = 8\text{ m}\), the pit is located \(13\text{ m} - 8\text{ m} = 5\text{ m}\) ahead.
In the next cycle, the drunkard takes 5 consecutive forward steps in \(5\text{ s}\), reaching \(8\text{ m} + 5\text{ m} = 13\text{ m}\) and falling into the pit immediately.
Total time taken:
\[T = 32\text{ s} + 5\text{ s} = 37\text{ s}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The drunkard falls into the pit after \(37\text{ s}\).

Final Answer:
37 s

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q36 - Relative impact speed of fired bullet

questiontext.text: A police van traveling on a highway with a speed of \(30\text{ km h}^{-1}\) fires a bullet at a thief's car fleeing in the same direction with a speed of \(192\text{ km h}^{-1}\). If the muzzle speed of the bullet relative to the van is \(150\text{ m s}^{-1}\), with what speed does the bullet strike the thief's car?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Van speed: \(v_{\text{van}} = 30\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Thief speed: \(v_{\text{thief}} = 192\text{ km h}^{-1}\). Muzzle speed: \(v_{\text{rel, muzzle}} = 150\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Convert speeds using \(1\text{ km h}^{-1} = \frac{5}{18}\text{ m s}^{-1}\).
Bullet speed relative to ground: \(v_{\text{bullet}} = v_{\text{rel, muzzle}} + v_{\text{van}}\).
Impact speed on thief's car: \(v_{\text{impact}} = v_{\text{bullet}} - v_{\text{thief}}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Convert vehicle speeds:
\[v_{\text{van}} = 30 \times \frac{5}{18} = \frac{25}{3}\text{ m s}^{-1}\]
\[v_{\text{thief}} = 192 \times \frac{5}{18} = \frac{160}{3}\text{ m s}^{-1}\]
Bullet speed relative to ground:
\[v_{\text{bullet}} = 150 + \frac{25}{3}\text{ m s}^{-1}\]
Impact speed:
\[v_{\text{impact}} = \left(150 + \frac{25}{3}\right) - \frac{160}{3} = 150 - \frac{135}{3} = 150 - 45 = 105\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The bullet hits the thief's car with an impact speed of \(105\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
105 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Chronological stages of vertically projected ball

questiontext.text:
A ball is thrown vertically upwards from ground level with an initial speed \(v_0\) under the influence of uniform gravity (air resistance is neglected). Consider the following stages of its motion:

  1. The ball reaches its uppermost point where its instantaneous velocity becomes zero while its acceleration remains \(-g\).
  2. The ball is projected upward and its speed continuously decreases due to downward gravitational acceleration.
  3. The ball strikes the ground at its initial projection level with a downward velocity of magnitude \(v_0\).
  4. The ball moves downward from the peak with increasing speed in the negative direction.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these stages from launch until the ball returns to the ground?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A projectile thrown vertically upward moves in a straight line under constant downward acceleration due to gravity (\(a = -g\)). The entire trajectory consists of an upward ascent followed by a downward descent.

Step 2: Evaluation of Upward Motion
At the moment of launch, the ball possesses an initial upward velocity \(v_0\). As it ascends, the downward gravitational acceleration continuously reduces its speed: \[ v(t) = v_0 - gt \] Thus, the upward ascent with decreasing speed occurs first among the listed stages.

Step 3: Evaluation of the Peak
When the upward speed diminishes completely to zero at time \(t = \frac{v_0}{g}\), the ball reaches its highest point. At this highest point, the instantaneous velocity is momentarily zero, while the downward acceleration remains \(g\). This peak occurs immediately after the upward ascent.

Step 4: Evaluation of Downward Motion and Ground Impact
After momentarily pausing at the apex, the ball begins to fall freely in the negative direction. Its speed increases linearly downward: \[ v(t) = -g(t - t_{\text{peak}}) \] Finally, upon descending through the same vertical height, the ball reaches the ground level where its velocity magnitude returns to \(v_0\) directed downward, terminating the flight.

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The chronological order of events is: upward ascent with decreasing speed, followed by reaching the peak with zero velocity, followed by downward descent with increasing speed, and finally striking the ground with speed \(v_0\). This corresponds to the sequence II → I → IV → III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Derivation steps of kinematic velocity relation

questiontext.text:
Consider the derivation of the kinematic equation \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)\) for uniformly accelerated rectilinear motion using differential calculus. The following mathematical steps are involved:

  1. Separate the variables to express the differential equation as \(v\,\mathrm{d}v = a\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  2. Apply the chain rule of differentiation to write acceleration as \(a = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = v\frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x}\).
  3. Integrate both sides using standard formulas to obtain \(\frac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2} = a(x - x_0)\).
  4. Set up definite integrals on both sides from initial state \((x_0, v_0)\) to final state \((x, v)\): \(\int_{v_0}^{v} v\,\mathrm{d}v = \int_{x_0}^{x} a\,\mathrm{d}x\).
  5. Rearrange the evaluated terms algebraically to obtain \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0)\).

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of steps for this derivation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
To derive the relation between velocity, uniform acceleration, and position without explicitly involving time \(t\), instantaneous acceleration \(a = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t}\) must be transformed using differential calculus and integrated over the limits of motion.

Step 2: Chain Rule Transformation
The derivation begins by expressing acceleration in terms of position coordinate \(x\) using the chain rule: \[ a = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \] Since \(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = v\), this yields: \[ a = v \frac{\mathrm{d}v}{\mathrm{d}x} \] This represents the primary defining step.

Step 3: Separation of Variables and Setting Integrals
Multiplying both sides by the spatial differential \(\mathrm{d}x\) separates the velocity and position variables: \[ v\,\mathrm{d}v = a\,\mathrm{d}x \] Next, definite integrals are established across both sides with consistent physical limits corresponding to the motion from \((x_0, v_0)\) at \(t = 0\) to \((x, v)\) at time \(t\): \[ \int_{v_0}^{v} v\,\mathrm{d}v = \int_{x_0}^{x} a\,\mathrm{d}x \]

Step 4: Integration and Algebraic Rearrangement
Because acceleration \(a\) is constant, it is factored out of the integral: \[ \left[\frac{v^2}{2}\right]_{v_0}^{v} = a [x]_{x_0}^{x} \implies \frac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2} = a(x - x_0) \] Finally, multiplying by 2 and transposing \(v_0^2\) yields the familiar kinematic formula: \[ v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a(x - x_0) \]

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct logical progression of steps is: chain rule representation, separation of variables, setting up definite integrals, performing the integration, and rearranging the terms. This corresponds to the sequence II → I → IV → III → V.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Numerical steps for finding instantaneous velocity

questiontext.text:
In kinematics, when an analytical position function \(x(t)\) is known, the instantaneous velocity at an instant \(t_0\) can be obtained by a numerical limiting process over smaller and smaller time intervals. Consider the following procedural steps:

  1. Compute the displacement \(\Delta x = x(t_2) - x(t_1)\) and the average velocity ratio \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) over the chosen interval.
  2. Select an initial finite time interval \(\Delta t\) centered symmetrically at \(t_0\), defining boundaries \(t_1 = t_0 - \frac{\Delta t}{2}\) and \(t_2 = t_0 + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\).
  3. Identify the unique limiting numerical value approached by \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) as the instantaneous velocity \(\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\) at \(t_0\).
  4. Calculate the position coordinates \(x(t_1)\) and \(x(t_2)\) using the given position-time function.
  5. Repeatedly shrink \(\Delta t\) (for example, from \(2.0\text{ s}\) to \(1.0\text{ s}\), \(0.1\text{ s}\), and \(0.01\text{ s}\)) and recalculate the ratio \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\).

Which of the following represents the correct procedural sequence of steps to determine the instantaneous velocity?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Instantaneous velocity is defined mathematically as the limit of average velocity as the time interval \(\Delta t\) approaches zero: \[ v(t_0) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} \] The numerical method systematically tabulates this ratio for progressively decreasing time intervals centered at \(t_0\).

Step 2: Defining Interval Boundaries and Computing Coordinates
First, a finite time interval \(\Delta t\) is chosen centered at the instant of interest \(t_0\), giving the initial time \(t_1 = t_0 - \frac{\Delta t}{2}\) and final time \(t_2 = t_0 + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\).
Next, substituting \(t_1\) and \(t_2\) into the position function gives the positions \(x(t_1)\) and \(x(t_2)\).

Step 3: Calculating Initial Average Velocity
The displacement \(\Delta x = x(t_2) - x(t_1)\) is evaluated, and the average velocity \(\bar{v} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) is calculated for this initial duration.

Step 4: Systematic Reduction of Time Interval and Convergence
To evaluate the limit, \(\Delta t\) is systematically reduced (e.g., \(2.0\text{ s} \to 1.0\text{ s} \to 0.5\text{ s} \to 0.1\text{ s} \to 0.01\text{ s}\)), recalculating the corresponding values of \(\Delta x\) and \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) at each reduction.
Finally, the limiting numerical value to which \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) converges as \(\Delta t \to 0\) is recognized as the exact value of the instantaneous velocity at \(t_0\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
The correct procedural sequence is: selecting centered interval boundaries, evaluating positions from the function, computing displacement and average velocity, repeatedly shrinking the interval, and finally identifying the converged limit. This corresponds to the sequence II → IV → I → V → III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_SEQUENCING_Q04 - Chronological phases of vehicle stopping process

questiontext.text:
A vehicle is travelling at a constant cruising speed \(v_0\) along a straight road when the driver suddenly spots an obstacle ahead at time \(t = 0\). Consider the following stages that occur until the vehicle comes to a complete halt:

  1. The vehicle undergoes uniform deceleration \(-a\) caused by braking, with speed decreasing linearly from \(v_0\) to zero.
  2. The driver observes the unexpected hazard and decides to apply the brakes during an elapsed reaction time \(t_r\).
  3. The vehicle comes to a complete rest (\(v = 0\)) having traversed a total stopping distance \(d_{\text{total}} = v_0 t_r + \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\).
  4. The vehicle covers a reaction distance \(d_r = v_0 t_r\) while maintaining its constant initial velocity \(v_0\).
  5. The vehicle covers a braking distance \(d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}\) under the active braking force.

Which of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of these physical stages from the instant the obstacle is first sighted?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The stopping process of a moving vehicle is divided into two distinct physical phases: the reaction phase (motion with constant velocity) and the braking phase (motion with constant deceleration).

Step 2: Analysis of the Reaction Phase
At \(t = 0\), the driver spots the obstacle. During the reaction time \(t_r\), the driver observes, thinks, and physically moves their foot to press the brake pedal. Because the brakes have not yet engaged, the vehicle continues to move with its initial cruising speed \(v_0\), covering a distance: \[ d_r = v_0 t_r \] Thus, observing the hazard during the reaction time occurs first, and covering the reaction distance accompanies this initial period.

Step 3: Analysis of the Braking Phase
Once the brake pedal is depressed, the braking mechanism activates, producing a uniform deceleration \(-a\). During this active deceleration, the vehicle's speed decreases continuously from \(v_0\) according to: \[ v(t) = v_0 - a t' \] While decelerating, the vehicle traverses the braking distance: \[ d_s = \frac{v_0^2}{2a} \]

Step 4: Complete Stop
When the velocity reaches zero, the motion ceases completely. The total stopping distance achieved at this terminal moment is the sum of the reaction distance and the braking distance: \[ d_{\text{total}} = d_r + d_s = v_0 t_r + \frac{v_0^2}{2a} \]

Step 5: Final Conclusion
Chronologically, the driver first observes the hazard during the reaction time, during which the vehicle traverses the reaction distance at constant speed. Next, deceleration commences, covering the braking distance, until the vehicle finally comes to rest with total stopping distance achieved. This corresponds to the sequence II → IV → I → V → III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q01 - Point object approximation in kinematics

questiontext.text: In the study of kinematics, an object in rectilinear motion can be treated to a good approximation as a point object if:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An object can be modeled as a point object whenever its linear dimensions or spatial extent are negligible compared to the total distance it traverses over a reasonable time duration.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
Treating a macroscopic body as a point object neglects rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom and internal deformations, which is valid only when the path length traversed is orders of magnitude larger than the body's size.

Final Answer:
The linear dimensions of the body are much smaller than the distance moved by it in a reasonable duration of time.

answer.text: its linear dimensions are much smaller than the distance moved by it in a reasonable duration of time
it moves strictly vertically under the sole influence of gravity
its total mass is zero while occupying a finite volume in space
it moves strictly with constant velocity and zero acceleration

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q02 - Identifying valid point object approximation

questiontext.text: Based on the point object approximation, in which of the following real-life situations can the moving body be considered approximately a point object?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A body can be treated as a point particle if its physical size is negligible compared to the distance it travels, and its internal rotational or tumbling motions do not significantly affect the description of its translational trajectory.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
A railway carriage traveling smoothly along a track between two distant stations covers several kilometers, which is enormously larger than the length or height of the carriage. In contrast, a tumbling beaker slipping off a table, a sharply spinning cricket ball, or a diver performing somersaults have sizes comparable to the distances involved or exhibit predominant rotational effects that cannot be neglected.

Final Answer:
A railway carriage moving smoothly without jerks between two distant stations.

answer.text: A spinning cricket ball that turns sharply on hitting the pitch
A railway carriage moving smoothly without jerks between two distant stations
A tumbling beaker that has slipped off the edge of a classroom table
A gymnast performing rapid somersaults over a vaulting horse

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q03 - Definition and scope of kinematics

questiontext.text: In physics, the branch of classical mechanics known as kinematics is specifically concerned with:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Kinematics is the branch of mechanics that describes the motion of points, bodies, and systems of bodies without considering the forces or causes that produce the motion.

Step 2: Physical Evaluation
The study of the forces and causes of changes in motion is the subject of dynamics, whereas statics deals with bodies in mechanical equilibrium.

Final Answer:
Describing the motion of objects without inquiring into the causes of motion.

answer.text: analyzing the forces and torques that cause changes in motion
determining the conditions of mechanical equilibrium under balanced forces
describing the motion of objects without inquiring into the causes of motion
investigating the microscopic and atomic deformations within moving bodies

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q04 - Instantaneous velocity from position function

questiontext.text: The position of an object moving along the \(x\)-axis is given by \(x = a + bt^2\), where \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), and \(t\) is measured in seconds. What is the instantaneous velocity of the object at \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The position function is \(x(t) = a + bt^2\) with constants \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\) and \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). The instant of interest is \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Instantaneous velocity is defined as the time derivative of position: \(v = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiating the position function with respect to time:
\[v = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(a + bt^2) = 0 + 2bt = 2bt\]
Substituting \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\) and \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\):
\[v = 2 \times 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2} \times 2.0\text{ s} = 10\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The units are meters per second, and at \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\), the velocity evaluates to \(10\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
10 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q05 - Average velocity from position function

questiontext.text: The position of an object moving along the \(x\)-axis is given by \(x = a + bt^2\), where \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\), and \(t\) is measured in seconds. What is the average velocity of the object over the time interval between \(t = 2.0\text{ s}\) and \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Position function: \(x(t) = a + bt^2\) with \(a = 8.5\text{ m}\), \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\). Initial time \(t_1 = 2.0\text{ s}\), final time \(t_2 = 4.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Average velocity over a time interval \([t_1, t_2]\) is given by the total displacement divided by the elapsed time:
\[\bar{v} = \frac{x(t_2) - x(t_1)}{t_2 - t_1}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate position at \(t_1 = 2.0\text{ s}\):
\[x(2.0) = a + b(2.0)^2 = a + 4b\]
Calculate position at \(t_2 = 4.0\text{ s}\):
\[x(4.0) = a + b(4.0)^2 = a + 16b\]
Find the displacement:
\[\Delta x = x(4.0) - x(2.0) = (a + 16b) - (a + 4b) = 12b\]
The time interval is \(\Delta t = 4.0\text{ s} - 2.0\text{ s} = 2.0\text{ s}\).
Evaluate average velocity:
\[\bar{v} = \frac{12b}{2.0} = 6.0b\]
Substitute \(b = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}\):
\[\bar{v} = 6.0 \times 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2} = 15\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The resulting average velocity is \(15\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
15 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q06 - Limiting value of average velocity

questiontext.text: A car moves along a straight road such that its position is given by \(x = 0.08 t^3\), where \(x\) is in meters and \(t\) is in seconds. The average velocity \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) is computed over successively shrinking time intervals centered at \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\). In the mathematical limit as \(\Delta t \to 0\), the value of \(\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\) converges to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The position function is \(x(t) = 0.08 t^3\). The instant of evaluation is \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By definition, the limit of the average velocity as \(\Delta t \to 0\) is the instantaneous velocity, which equals the first derivative of position with respect to time:
\[v = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\]

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Differentiating \(x(t)\) with respect to time:
\[\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}(0.08 t^3) = 3 \times 0.08 t^2 = 0.24 t^2\]
Evaluating at \(t = 4.0\text{ s}\):
\[v(4.0) = 0.24 \times (4.0)^2 = 0.24 \times 16 = 3.84\text{ m s}^{-1}\]

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
The limiting value of the average velocity as the interval approaches zero is \(3.84\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Final Answer:
3.84 m s^{-1}

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q07 - Instantaneous speed and magnitude of velocity

questiontext.text: Although average speed over a finite time interval can be strictly greater than the magnitude of average velocity, instantaneous speed at any instant is always equal to the magnitude of instantaneous velocity. Which of the following statements provides the correct physical justification?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Speed is defined as the rate of covering distance (path length), while velocity is the rate of change of displacement.

Step 2: Evaluation and Application
Over a finite interval, an object may reverse direction or move along a curved path, making path length greater than magnitude of displacement. However, as the time interval \(\Delta t\) becomes infinitesimally small (\(\Delta t \to 0\)), the path of the particle between two consecutive instants becomes a straight line segment without any possibility of reversal. Consequently, the infinitesimal path length \(\mathrm{d}s\) becomes exactly equal to the magnitude of the infinitesimal displacement \(|\mathrm{d}x|\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(\frac{\mathrm{d}s}{\mathrm{d}t} = \left|\frac{\mathrm{d}x}{\mathrm{d}t}\right|\), establishing that instantaneous speed is identically equal to the magnitude of instantaneous velocity.

Final Answer:
In the infinitesimal limit as time interval approaches zero, the infinitesimal path length equals the magnitude of the infinitesimal displacement.

answer.text: The acceleration of the particle becomes identically zero over an infinitesimal time interval
Instantaneous velocity is a scalar quantity that has no assigned algebraic sign or direction
In the limit \(\Delta t \to 0\), the infinitesimal path length becomes identical to the magnitude of the infinitesimal displacement
A particle cannot change its acceleration over any finite duration of motion

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_MOTION_IN_A_STRAIGHT_LINE_MCQ_Q08 - Relation between average speed and average velocity

questiontext.text: For an object in one-dimensional rectilinear motion over a given time interval, which of the following relations correctly connects the average speed \(\bar{v}_{\text{speed}}\) and the magnitude of average velocity \(|\bar{v}_{\text{velocity}}|\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Average speed is total path length divided by total time interval, whereas the magnitude of average velocity is the magnitude of net displacement divided by total time interval.
